title: Mechanosensing channels PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 regulate mitral valve serotonin-mediated homeostasis and pathophysiology
authors: Emily Hall
abstract: Mitral regurgitation (MR) pathophysiology involves increased serotonin (5-HT) receptor (HTR) expression and signalling, together with reduced 5-HT transporter (SLC6A4) expression in mitral valve interstitial cells (MVIC). The mechanosensitive calcium channels, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, regulate cellular responses to a variety of mechanical conditions; however, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 have not been studied in MR. We investigated the hypothesis that PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 mediate, through 5-HT mechanisms, both homeostasis in normal mitral valves (nMV) and in the pathophysiology of MR.

title: Salvaging the forgotten valve: T-TEER as the new frontier in torrential primary TR
authors: Nazario Carrabba; Mattia Alexis Amico; A Taddei; Renato Valenti; Alfredo Giuseppe Cerillo; Pierluigi Stefàno
abstract: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) has historically been considered the “forgotten valve disease”, but growing evidence has established its independent prognostic impact and has driven the rapid expansion of transcatheter tricuspid valve interventions. While transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) has demonstrated safety and clinical benefit in patients with secondary functional TR, evidence supporting its use in primary TR remains scarce, and surgery continues to represent the standard treatment. However, many patients with primary TR are considered ineligible for surgery because of prohibitive operative risk, creating an important unmet therapeutic need. In this Perspective, we discuss the potential role of T-TEER in selected patients with primary TR through the paradigm of a patient who developed torrential TR following iatrogenic rupture of the septal papillary muscle–chordal apparatus during cardiac device lead extraction. Owing to multiple comorbidities and prohibitive surgical risk, the patient underwent successful transcatheter repair with two PASCAL Ace devices, achieving durable TR reduction and sustained clinical improvement at one-year follow-up. Building on this experience, we review the current evidence supporting transcatheter tricuspid interventions, discuss the anatomical and procedural considerations that may enable T-TEER in selected forms of primary TR, and highlight the limitations of the available literature. We propose that carefully selected anatomical subsets of primary TR may represent an emerging frontier for transcatheter therapies, bridging the gap between guideline-directed management and individualized treatment when surgery is not feasible. Prospective studies are warranted to define patient selection criteria, procedural feasibility, and long-term clinical outcomes.

title: Anticoagulation with Bivalirudin in a Case of Mitral Valve Replacement and Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Requiring Prolonged Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Support: A Case of Emergency Surgery Due to Posterior Papillary Muscle Rupture
authors: Sedef Dündar; Cihan Yücel; Mücahit Ergin; Serkan Ketenciler
abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is an increasingly used support method in cases of refractory cardiopulmonary failure. However, due to the non-biological surfaces of the system and the inflammatory responses it induces, coagulation disorders may develop, necessitating meticulous anticoagulation management. At present, unfractionated heparin (UFH) is used as the standard; however, in complications such as heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), alternative agents may be required. We present the management of a 59-yearold male who developed acute mitral regurgitation due to posterior papillary muscle rupture and underwent emergency mitral valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting. Due to post-operative right ventricular failure, venoarterial ECMO support was initiated. On the 5 th day of ECMO, progressive thrombocytopenia and central catheter thrombosis occurred. With a high 4T score, HIT was suspected. UFH infusion was discontinued, and bivalirudin was initiated as an alternative anticoagulant. The anticoagulation process was monitored with activated clotting time and activated partial thromboplastin time, and therapeutic targets were successfully achieved without major bleeding or thrombotic complications. The patient was weaned off ECMO on day 15 and discharged in stable condition on post-operative day 74. This case demonstrates that bivalirudin is a safe and effective anticoagulant option in ECMO patients who develop HIT. In complex cases with heparin contraindications, bivalirudin plays an important role in individualized anticoagulation strategies.

title: Case Report: Impella CP-protected percutaneous coronary intervention of the last remaining vessel—a LIMA-to-LAD graft—complicated by no-reflow and rescued with a drug-coated balloon
authors: Fotios Toulgaridis; Stavros Tzortzis; Nikolaos Tsiamis; Konstantinos Sassalos; Nikolaos Karanikolas; Ioannis Mavrogenis; Anastasia N. Kitsiou; Georgios Triantis
abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the last remaining conduit in a patient with severely impaired left ventricular function is among the most hazardous procedures in contemporary interventional cardiology, as any interruption of flow essentially constitutes a global ischemic insult. We describe a 77-year-old man, a former heavy smoker with an 80-pack-year smoking history, who had undergone three-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 22 years previously. His medical history also included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25–30%, and severe mitral regurgitation (MR). At presentation, he had Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III angina and New York Heart Association class III symptoms. The most recent coronary angiogram, performed 6 months earlier, demonstrated chronic total occlusion (CTO) of both saphenous vein grafts, in addition to CTO of all three native epicardial coronary arteries. Thus, the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft to the left anterior descending artery (LAD) represented the sole functional conduit, directly perfusing the LAD territory and supplying the right coronary and circumflex territories through primarily septal and epicardial collaterals, respectively. The LAD displayed two sequential severe stenoses (≥80% each), one at the distal LIMA–LAD anastomosis and another further distally in the native vessel. In accordance with current coronary revascularization guidelines, the Heart Team recommended evaluation by cardiac surgeons. Two independent cardiothoracic surgeons declined redo CABG as a viable therapeutic option. Complex and high-risk indicated PCI (CHIP) was therefore considered the only feasible revascularization strategy. Additional hemodynamic support with percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (pMCS) was deemed necessary. Residual MR and arrhythmic risk, including the potential indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), were planned to be reassessed 3 months after successful percutaneous revascularization. CHIP was performed under full hemodynamic support with a continuous-flow microaxial pump (Impella CP with SmartAssist) inserted via the left femoral artery, while coronary intervention was performed through the ipsilateral radial artery using a 6-F IMA guiding catheter. The lesions were successfully crossed with a workhorse wire, despite substantial technical difficulty and with the aid of a microcatheter; however, distal flow was immediately lost, and intracoronary nitroglycerin failed to restore it. Balloon angioplasty restored flow only partially, and a decision was made to proceed with stent implantation. However, stent delivery proved challenging, requiring a guide-extension catheter to be advanced deep into the LIMA body using the so-called ‘inchworming technique.’ Despite successful implantation of the first drug-eluting stent (DES) at the distal anastomotic lesion, a second DES could not be advanced to the more distal native LAD lesion, despite the use of multiple guidewires and supportive guiding-catheter strategies. Therefore, a drug-coated balloon (DCB) was used as a bailout strategy, immediately restoring TIMI grade 3 flow and leaving only a minor, non-flow-limiting type B dissection. Impella support was discontinued early because of access-related left lower-limb ischemia, and successful percutaneous hemostasis was achieved using a suture-based closure technique. Peak high-sensitivity troponin I, measured the following evening, was 10,800 pg/mL. The patient was discharged ambulatory on day 2 and remained asymptomatic at 3-month follow-up, when an ICD was implanted for primary prevention. This case illustrates the critical role of pMCS in maintaining hemodynamic stability when native coronary flow is lost during PCI of the last remaining conduit and highlights the value of DCB angioplasty as a bailout strategy when stent delivery is not feasible.

title: Decision tree models to guide endotracheal tube selection in dogs
authors: Nuttawadee Ngamlertwong; Veerasak Punyapornwithaya; Supitchaya Siriyakhun; Chris Seymour; Seri SEKI
abstract: Introduction Choosing an endotracheal tube (ETT) of an appropriate size is critical for effective airway management in dogs undergoing anesthesia or emergency care. Conventional methods often rely on body weight (BW), palpation of external tracheal diameter, nasal septum width, or subjective clinician experience. However, these approaches are frequently imprecise and lack well-established guidelines. Therefore, this study aimed to develop a machine learning-based decision tree model to standardize ETT size using measurable anatomical parameters in dolichocephalic, mesocephalic, and brachycephalic breeds. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on data from dogs undergoing anesthesia or emergency care at the Northern Regional Veterinary Healthcare and Learning Center, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Chiang Mai University, (NOVEL CMU) Thailand between January and December 2024. We investigated the relationship between the internal diameter (ID) of the ETT used and multiple patient variables, including BW, sex, age, breed, and internal tracheal diameter (ITD) measured at the thoracic inlet on radiographs. Decision tree analysis was used to determine the ETT selection. We hypothesized that a decision tree model integrating BW and ITD would accurately predict appropriate ETT sizing in dogs, but that upper airway anatomical differences would necessitate separate models for non-brachycephalic breeds (Group DM, including dolichocephalic and mesocephalic conformation) and brachycephalic breeds (Group B). Results and discussion The results demonstrated that Group B required ETTs with a significantly smaller ID compared to Group DM of the same BW. Variable importance analysis identified BW and ITD as the primary predictors of ETT size in both groups. Conversely, sex and age demonstrated negligible predictive value and were not significant factors in the selection process. Hence, the decision tree model successfully generated distinct algorithmic pathways for Group DM and Group B. The developed decision tree models offer a practical, non-invasive method for standardizing ETT sizes in clinical practice, thereby enhancing skilled veterinary human capital. This algorithmic approach accounts for individual anatomical variations in the respiratory tract, particularly in brachycephalic dogs. For clinical application, clinicians should prepare tubes within ±0.5 mm of the predicted size to ensure optimal airway management and patient safety.

title: Anomalous Origin of the Left Coronary Artery from the Pulmonary Artery Beyond Infancy: Single-Center Experience of Clinical Spectrum and Surgical Outcomes
authors: Betül Çınar; Pelin Ayyıldız; Sertaç Haydın; Alper Güzeltaş
abstract: Objective: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) is a rare and life-threatening congenital anomaly. While it typically manifests during early infancy, some patients remain asymptomatic or present later in childhood and adolescence due to well-developed intercoronary collaterals. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the clinical spectrum, diagnostic features, and surgical outcomes of patients diagnosed with ALCAPA beyond infancy at our center. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on 35 patients diagnosed with ALCAPA who underwent surgical treatment at our center between January 2012 and January 2025. Out of this cohort, 8 patients diagnosed beyond infancy (older than 12 months) were enrolled in this study to evaluate their clinical spectrum and surgical revascularization outcomes. Results: The age at diagnosis ranged from 2 to 21 years (median: 6.8 years), and all patients were female. Four patients (50%) were completely asymptomatic at presentation. Symptomatic presentations included exertional chest pain (n=1), recurrent vomiting and irritability (n=2), and sudden cardiac arrest with sustained ventricular arrhythmia (n=1). Electrocardiography (ECG) revealed characteristic ALCAPA patterns in 5 patients. Echocardiography demonstrated left ventricular (LV) and right coronary artery (RCA) dilation in all cases, with a mean RCA/aortic annulus ratio of 0.25. Baseline LV systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction: 30–45%) was observed in 4 patients. Surgical management consisted of direct coronary reimplantation (n=6) and the Takeuchi procedure (n=2). Mitral valve repair was performed in 2 patients with structural mitral anomalies. At a mean follow-up of 48 months, all patients were alive and asymptomatic, with full recovery of LV function and resolution of ECG abnormalities within 6–9 months postoperatively. Conclusion: ALCAPA must be considered in the differential diagnosis of unexplained LV dilation or mitral regurgitation across all pediatric age groups. Extensive collateral circulation can mask typical features, leading to atypical presentations or misdiagnosis. Prompt establishment of a dual-coronary system provides a satisfactoryprognosis and facilitates complete myocardial recovery.

title: Early Hemodynamic and Clinical Outcomes of Aortic Valve Neocuspidization for Severe Aortic Stenosis: A Single-Center Experience
authors: Safa Özçelik; Benay Erden
abstract: Objective: Aortic valve neocuspidization using autologous pericardium is a reconstructive option for aortic valve disease. We evaluated the early hemodynamic and clinical outcomes of the Ozaki procedure in a single-center cohort. Methods: This retrospective study included 31 consecutive patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent aortic valve neocuspidization between January 2023 and June 2025. Pre-operative and 6-month echocardiographic findings were compared in 30 patients with paired data. Clinical outcomes were assessed through at least 12 months of follow-up among surviving patients. Results: Median age was 65.0 years, and seven patients (22.6%) underwent a concomitant cardiac procedure. The median mean transvalvular gradient decreased from 50.5 mmHg preoperatively to 9.0 mmHg at 6 months (p<0.001). The maximum gradient decreased from 83.0 to 18.0 mmHg, and peak aortic jet velocity decreased from 4.60 to 1.85 m/s (both p<0.001). At 6 months, aortic regurgitation was absent in 16 patients (53.3%), mild in 12 (40.0%), and moderate in two (6.7%); none had severe regurgitation. One patient (3.2%) died during the index hospitalization. Another developed infective endocarditis with acute severe aortic regurgitation at 9 months and subsequently died. Overall 1-year survival was 93.5%. Conclusion: Aortic valve neocuspidization was associated with low transvalvular gradients and generally favorable valve competence at 6 months. The fatal endocarditis event underscores the need for continued surveillance. Larger studies with longer follow-up are needed to assess durability.

title: Efficacy of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on functional mitral regurgitation associated with heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
authors: Charlie Kajo; Ahmed J. AlAraibi; Osama T Almutairi; Yaqeen H. Alaraibi; Abdullah A. Alibrahim; Yousef Kh A Almutawah; Salem  W. S. Alasfar; Mustafa  Wasif Ali; Aseel Hajjiri; Mohammad Alqaryuti; Abdullatif Alfehaid; Dana Z. Arekat
abstract: Background Functional mitral regurgitation (FMR) commonly complicates heart failure (HF) and portends a poor prognosis. While sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) improve clinical outcomes and induce cardiac reverse remodeling in HF, their specific effect on FMR associated with HF severity remains uncertain. Methods Five databases were searched from inception to 21 July 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating SGLT2i in adult patients with HF and chronic FMR on background guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). Primary outcomes were changes from baseline in effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) and regurgitant volume (RV). Secondary clinical outcomes included HF hospitalization and cardiovascular (CVS) death. Random-effects models were used. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Results Three RCTs involving 455patients were included. SGLT2i therapy was associated with a statistically significant reduction in EROA (MD −0.086 cm 2 , 95% CI −0.150 to −0.022) and RV (MD −10.87 mL, 95% CI −17.32 to −4.43), but substantial heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 72.5% and I 2 = 63.5%, respectively). On leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, statistical significance for both primary valvular outcomes was lost after omitting the EFFORT trial. The certainty of evidence was rated as low. Conclusion Addition of SGLT2i to GDMT was associated with reductions in FMR severity in pooled analyses; however, these findings were not robust in sensitivity analyses and are limited by low certainty of evidence. The apparent reduction in clinical events requires cautious interpretation due to event sparsity. These results should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, warranting further validation in large-scale, prospective trials. title: Initial Clip Selection and Outcomes After Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair: A Single-Center Experience
authors: Aysel Akhundova; Berhan Keskin; Ümeyir Savur; Ozlem Onder; Ebubekir Yiğitbay; Ekrem Guler; Hacı Murat Güneş; Mehmet Emir Arman; Bilal Boztosun
abstract: Background: Whether the initial clip type selected during transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) of the mitral valve—grasping width and arm length—independently influences procedural and echocardiographic outcomes remains uncertain. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 138 consecutive patients undergoing mitral TEER. The first implanted clip was classified as narrow standard-length (NT), long narrow-arm (XT), or long wide-arm (XTW). Determinants of initial clip selection and its association with procedural success (residual mitral regurgitation [MR] ≤ 1+), post-procedural transmitral gradient, and the need for ≥2 clips were assessed using multivariable logistic and linear regression. Results: Median age was 74.0 (66.0–80.0), 74.5 (66.0–82.5), and 75.0 (70.0–79.0) years, and median LVEF was 35.0% (30.0–50.0), 30.0% (25.0–45.0), and 40.0% (25.0–45.0), for the NT, XT, and XTW groups, respectively; 66% of patients overall were male. An XTW clip was implanted first in 61.6% of patients. XTW selection was independently associated with larger effective regurgitant orifice area, lower LVEF, longer posterior leaflet length, and secondary MR (all p < 0.05), whereas NT selection favored younger age, smaller orifice, and higher LVEF. After adjustment for these factors, no statistically significant independent association was detected between initial clip type and residual MR ≥2+, post-procedural transmitral gradient, or the need for additional clips (all p > 0.05); however, confidence intervals were wide. On univariable analysis, larger left atrial size and moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation were associated with residual MR ≥ 2+, but neither remained significant after multivariable adjustment. Conclusions: Initial clip selection was associated with valve anatomy, LVEF and MR etiology. No statistically significant independent association between initial clip type and procedural or short-term echocardiographic outcomes was detected in this cohort. Given the observational design, confounding by indication, limited sample size and wide confidence intervals, clinically relevant effects cannot be excluded, and these findings do not establish the superiority or equivalence of any clip-selection strategy.

title: Pre-existing cardiovascular disease and critical illness recovery: A multi-method study of the impact and experiences of patients and relatives
authors: Nicola Mary Anne Rea
journal: Edinburgh Napier Research Repository (Edinburgh Napier University)
abstract: Background: Approximately 25% of critically ill patients have pre-existing CVD. Research has shown that pre-critical illness health and the presence of co-morbidities are linked to adverse outcomes. Yet, little is known about the impact of pre-existing CVD or how it is managed during critical illness recovery. Aim: To explore the role of pre-existing CVD in determining recovery outcomes, experiences, and support needs beyond the hospital setting for critical illness survivors and their relatives. Methods: This thesis adopted a pragmatic multi-method approach comprising three studies. First, a systematic review explored experiences and perspectives of physical symptoms in the context of follow-up care. It employed a reflexive thematic analysis approach. Second, a retrospective observational cohort study investigated the impact of pre-existing CVD on emergency critical care survivors. A binary logistic regression using multiple imputation was run with one-year hospital readmission as the primary outcome. Third, a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews explored the perspectives of critical illness survivors with pre-existing CVD and their relatives on experiences of recovery and support. Findings: The systematic review (n=11) highlighted that baseline health influences how patients perceive recovery, and that follow-up care often fails to address pre-existing co-morbidities. The quantitative study (n=51,625) found pre-existing CVD was prevalent (17.1%) and is associated with higher hospital readmission rates (OR 1.20). The qualitative study (n=12) identified Post-Intensive Care Syndrome is the dominant factor in short-term recovery rather than pre-existing CVD. Further, it emphasised the need for active involvement of patients and relatives in care. Conclusion: Pre-existing CVD may be clinically relevant, yet from a patient perspective, priorities and support are misaligned. Further, current healthcare service delivery does not adequately account for the importance of pre-existing CVD during critical illness recovery. This thesis has shown that pre-existing CVD may be associated with adverse outcomes and highlights a gap in care.

title: Remote monitoring in patients awaiting elective cardiac surgery is associated with improved clinical outcomes: a prospective service evaluation
authors: Arun Kirupananthavel; Martin T. Yates; Kulvinder S. Lall; Simon Woldman; Shivani Joshi; Nimra Ahsan; Adem Aktas; Gordon Ferguson; Nay Aung; Charles J. Knight; Andrew Wragg; Debashish Das; Stephen Edmondson
abstract: Abstract Background Rising elective cardiac surgery waiting times are associated with increased risk of clinical deterioration and unscheduled admissions. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) may offer earlier detection of deterioration, but its role during the pre-operative waiting period is not well established. Methods We conducted a prospective single centre service evaluation of a digital RPM pathway for adults listed for elective cardiac surgery between September 2022 and September 2023. Patients submitting at least one digital symptom questionnaire (activated group) were compared with those who did not (non-activated). Primary outcomes were preoperative mortality and unscheduled admissions requiring non elective intervention. Secondary outcomes included resternotomy, 1 year postoperative mortality, and length of stay. Results Of 1,164 patients, 799 (68.6%) were activated. Baseline characteristics were similar aside from higher hypertension and diabetes prevalence in the non-activated group. Pre-operative mortality was significantly lower in activated patients (0.6% vs 2.2%; RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09–0.87; p=0.018). Unscheduled admissions were also reduced (2.1% vs 4.3%; RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.25–0.95; p=0.031). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated early and sustained separation (log-rank p=0.012). Secondary outcomes were similar between groups. In the propensity-matched cohort, activation remained associated with lower pre-operative mortality (0.7% vs 3.5%; RR 0.20; p=0.027) and fewer unscheduled admissions (2.0% vs 5.8%; RR 0.35; p=0.026). Conclusion Implementation of a structured pre-operative RPM pathway was feasible at scale and associated with significantly reduced pre-operative mortality and fewer unplanned admissions. These findings support RPM as a promising strategy to enhance safety and stability for patients awaiting elective cardiac surgery.

title: Admission high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T and clinical outcomes after acute ischemic stroke: a retrospective cohort study with exploratory nonlinear analysis
authors: Yisheng Chen; Suhua Liu; Hua Xue; Rui Wang; Rongfang Wen; 肖兆祥; Xuerong Sheng; Peifeng Chen; Na Song; Yongkun Li
abstract: Background Elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) is frequently observed in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and has been associated with adverse outcomes. We aimed to evaluate the association of admission hs-cTnT with 90-day functional outcome and all-cause mortality during follow-up, with particular attention to potential nonlinear risk patterns across the biomarker range. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included 564 patients with AIS admitted between January 2022 and October 2024. The primary outcomes were modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 90 days and long-term all-cause mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was used for poor 90-day functional outcome and Cox proportional hazards models were used for all-cause mortality during follow-up. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were performed to explore nonlinear dose–response relationships, and segmented regression models were used to estimate exploratory turning points. Results Among 564 patients, 212 (37.6%) had elevated hs-cTnT (>14 ng/L). Elevated hs-cTnT was independently associated with poor 90-day mRS (adjusted OR 1.93, 95% CI, 1.22–3.05; p = 0.005) and all-cause mortality during follow-up (fully adjusted HR 4.12, 95% CI, 2.31–7.48; p < 0.001). During a median follow-up of 17 months (IQR 12–26 months), Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower overall survival in patients with elevated hs-cTnT ( p < 0.001). RCS analysis revealed significant nonlinear associations between hs-cTnT and both endpoints ( p < 0.001). Exploratory model-derived turning points were observed at 28.42 ng/L for functional outcome and 31.68 ng/L for mortality; these should be interpreted as exploratory rather than validated clinical cutoffs. Below these values, risk increased more steeply; above them, no statistically significant further increase in risk was observed. Conclusion Admission hs-cTnT was independently associated with 90-day functional outcome and all-cause mortality during follow-up in patients with AIS. The association appeared to be nonlinear, with model-derived turning points at approximately 28–32 ng/L that should be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive clinical cutoffs. Clinically, hs-cTnT may be useful as a complementary marker for identifying patients at higher risk who may warrant closer neuro-cardiac evaluation, although its incremental predictive value has not been formally assessed.

title: Association of pre-existing cardiovascular disease with cardiovascular and clinical outcomes in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors
authors: Lama Alfehaid; Ahmed S. Alanazi; Mansour Alomran; Hadi Skouri; Nada Alsuhebany
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer therapy but are increasingly associated with cardiovascular complications. The association between pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD) and cardiovascular outcomes among patients receiving ICIs remains incompletely characterized, particularly in real-world settings. To evaluate the association between baseline CVD and cardiovascular and clinical outcomes among adult patients treated with ICIs. We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study at two tertiary hospitals in Saudi Arabia, including adult patients who received at least one ICI dose between January 2017 and January 2023. Baseline CVD was defined as documented cardiovascular disease before ICI initiation. The primary outcome was a composite of new cardiovascular events occurring after ICI initiation. The secondary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used multivariable logistic regression to identify factors independently associated with cardiovascular events, with sensitivity analyses incorporating additional cardiovascular risk factors. Among 608 patients, 54 (8.9%) had baseline CVD. Patients with baseline CVD were older and had a greater burden of comorbidities than those without baseline CVD. During follow-up, 69 patients (11.3%) experienced at least one cardiovascular event. Cardiovascular events occurred in 27 of 54 patients (50.0%) with baseline CVD compared with 42 of 554 patients (7.6%) without baseline CVD ( p < 0.001). Baseline CVD was independently associated with higher odds of cardiovascular events (adjusted OR, 9.46; 95% CI 4.92–18.17; p < 0.001), and increasing age was also independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR per year, 1.04; 95% CI 1.01–1.06; p = 0.001). The association remained significant after additional adjustment for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and dyslipidemia (adjusted OR, 6.64; 95% CI 3.28–13.47; p < 0.001). All-cause mortality was higher among patients with baseline CVD (64.8% vs. 46.4%, p = 0.010), and unadjusted median overall survival was shorter (11.5 vs. 23.8 months; log-rank p = 0.022). Cardiovascular events were predominantly ischemic and heart failure-related, whereas myocarditis was rare, occurring in only one patient overall. In this multicenter cohort, pre-existing CVD was independently associated with higher cardiovascular event odds among ICI patients, even after adjusting for risk factors. These patients also had shorter OS, though survival analysis was unadjusted. Findings suggest baseline CVD patients are vulnerable and may benefit from thorough risk assessment and cardio-oncology care. However, as an observational study without a non-ICI comparator, these associations do not prove ICI caused or worsened CVD.

title: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis in peripheral neuropathy: prevalence, clinical features, and neurology-based screening in non-endemic Japan
authors: Yurika Okuma; Kenji Isahaya; Sachiko Ohori; Satomi Mitsuhashi; Tomoo Sato; Yoshihisa Yamano
abstract: Introduction Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) is a progressive, potentially fatal disease caused by pathogenic TTR variants. Although increasingly recognized as a cardiac disorder, ATTRv may initially present with peripheral neuropathy. Prospective data on the prevalence and clinical features of ATTRv among patients attending neurology clinics in non-endemic regions of Japan remain limited. Methods We prospectively enrolled 130 consecutive patients evaluated for suspected peripheral neuropathy at a neurology clinic in a non-endemic region of Japan between 2020 and 2025. The entire TTR coding region was analyzed by bidirectional Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA obtained from peripheral blood. Clinical, neurological, and cardiac findings were evaluated. Results Pathogenic TTR variants were identified in three patients (3/130, 2.31%; exact 95% CI, 0.5–6.6%): ATTRV122I [p.(Val142Ile)], ATTRI127V [p.(Ile147Val)], and ATTRV30M [p.(Val50Met)]. Two of the three variants were non-V30M variants unrelated to the Japanese endemic foci. All three patients had late-onset disease without a family history, with neurological manifestations ranging from established axonal or mixed polyneuropathy to early, mild involvement. Cardiac amyloid involvement was demonstrated in all three patients, including one with a structurally normal echocardiogram. A low-voltage electrocardiogram (ECG) was observed in all three ATTRv patients (3/3, 100%) compared with 5 of 95 (5.3%) variant-negative patients with available ECG data. Discussion ATTRv was identified in 2.31% of patients evaluated for suspected peripheral neuropathy in a non-endemic Japanese neurology clinic, a frequency comparable to that reported in European cohorts. These findings highlight the importance of considering ATTRv in patients with unexplained progressive neuropathy, even without a family history or residence in an endemic region, and support early TTR genetic testing when clinical red flags are present. The observation of low-voltage ECGs in all three ATTRv patients suggests that ECG may provide a complementary clue to occult cardiac involvement. However, this finding is preliminary and hypothesis-generating and requires validation in larger, independent prospective cohorts.

title: Frontal QRS-T angle in patients with Graves’ disease: association with thyroid function and cardiovascular parameters
authors: Maksymilian Kłosowicz; Magdalena Urbańczuk; Aleksandra Burbelka; Agnieszka Gala‐Błądzińska; Krzysztof Balawender
abstract: Introduction Thyroid hormone excess may alter ventricular electrophysiology, affecting both depolarization and repolarization. The frontal QRS-T (fQRS-T) angle reflects the directional relationship between these processes and may provide information on ventricular electrical heterogeneity. However, data on the fQRS-T angle in overt hyperthyroidism (OHT) remain limited. We evaluated the fQRS-T angle in patients with Graves’ disease presenting with OHT compared with euthyroid controls. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included 55 patients with Graves’ disease and biochemically confirmed OHT and 42 euthyroid controls. Frontal QRS and T axes were calculated from ECG measurements in leads I and aVF. Between-group comparisons, multivariable regression adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, and heart rate, sensitivity analyses, ROC analysis, and correlations with thyroid function parameters were performed. Results: The median fQRS-T angle was greater in patients with OHT than in controls (21.89° [12.37–44.09] vs. 17.36° [9.02–27.29], p = 0.006), with a rank-biserial correlation of 0.328 (95% CI 0.106–0.535). An fQRS-T angle >45° occurred in 23.6% of patients with OHT and in none of the controls (p < 0.001), whereas the QRS and T axes did not differ significantly between groups. After adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, and heart rate, OHT remained associated with a greater fQRS-T angle (β = 9.00°, 95% CI 1.77–16.22; p = 0.015), with consistent findings in sensitivity analyses. Discriminatory performance was modest (AUC 0.664, 95% CI 0.552–0.768). No significant associations were observed between fQRS-T angle and FT3, FT4, TSH, or heart rate. Discussion Patients with Graves’ disease and OHT exhibited greater discordance between ventricular depolarization and repolarization despite similar individual QRS and T axes. This association persisted after adjustment for heart rate and other potential confounders, suggesting that fQRS-T widening may reflect electrophysiological alterations associated with OHT rather than tachycardia alone. Conclusion Overt hyperthyroidism due to Graves’ disease is associated with a wider fQRS-T angle independently of age, sex, body mass index, and heart rate. Larger prospective, multicenter studies with longitudinal ECG assessment are needed to determine the reversibility and prognostic significance of these alterations.

title: Adiposity and the risk of aortic dissection incidence and mortality: results from the UK Biobank, the J-SHC study and a meta-analysis of cohort studies
authors: Alison Dillman; Yoichiro Otaki; M.R. Sánchez-Pérez; Momina Yawar Irfan Khan; Makoto Hibino; Tsuneo Konta; Kunihiro Yamagata; Shouichi Fujimoto; Kazuhiko Tsuruya; Ichiei Narita; Masato Kasahara; Yugo Shibagaki; Kunitoshi Iseki; Toshiki Moriyama; Masahide Kondo; Koichi Asahi; Tsuyoshi Watanabe; Tetsu Watanabe; Masafumi Watanabe; Dagfinn Aune
abstract: Abstract Few studies have investigated the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection and data is lacking on adiposity measures other than body mass index (BMI). We analyzed the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection in the UK Biobank, and the Japan Specific Health Checkups (J-SHC) Study, and conducted a meta-analysis of cohort studies to clarify the associations between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. The analytical cohorts included 496,255 participants in the UK Biobank and 630,841 participants in the J-SHC Study. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to analyze associations between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. PubMed and Embase were searched for relevant studies up to February 27, 2026. Random effects models were used to calculate summary relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between adiposity and risk of aortic dissection. In the UK Biobank and J-SHC, there were 371 and 105 aortic dissections during 12.3 and 4 years follow-up, respectively. In the UK Biobank, positive associations (HRs, 95% CIs) were observed between high BMI (1.54, 1.01–2.37, p trend =0.01), waist circumference (1.82, 1.27–2.60, p trend =0.001), hip circumference (1.77, 1.25–2.50, p trend <0.001), waist-to-height ratio (1.88, 1.30–2.70, p trend =0.10), and fat mass (1.36, 0.97–1.91, p trend =0.02) and aortic dissection risk, but no clear association was observed for waist-to-hip ratio (1.28, 0.90–1.81, p trend =0.08) and body fat percentage (1.09, 0.77–1.54, p trend =0.53). In the J-SHC Study, higher BMI (2.36, 0.98–4.84, p trend =0.018), waist circumference (2.26, 1.18–4.60, p trend =0.003), and waist-to-height ratio (2.61, 1.27–5.92, p trend =0.009) were positively associated with aortic dissection mortality. Five cohort studies were included in the meta-analysis on BMI and aortic dissection (2007 cases and 4,962,288 participants). The summary RR per 5 kg/m 2 increment in BMI was 1.09 (1.00-1.20, I 2 = 43%), per 10 cm increment in waist circumference was 1.21 (1.05–1.40, I 2 = 50%, n = 2), and per 0.1 unit increment in waist-to-height ratio was 1.32 (1.08–1.61, I 2 = 39%, n = 2). These findings provide evidence for a positive association between both general and abdominal adiposity and the risk of aortic dissection, with the strongest associations observed for high waist-to-height ratio. Although further large-scale studies are warranted for confirmation, these findings suggest avoiding excess weight may be an important strategy for the prevention of aortic dissection.

title: Biochemically supported diagnosis of Fabry disease in a young adult with unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy: a diagnostic challenge
authors: Noor Mohd Firdaus Othman; Hamizah Idrus; Sofwatul Mukhtaroh Nasohah; Ros Hamieza Mohd Yusoff; Siti Salbiah Norazan; Afif Ashari
abstract: Fabry disease (OMIM #301500) is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene, resulting in deficient activity of α-galactosidase A. This enzymatic defect leads to lysosomal glycosphingolipid accumulation and progressive multisystem dysfunction. The clinical manifestations are variable and non-specific, which may delay diagnosis. We report a 29-year-old Malay man who presented with recurrent palpitations, exertional chest pain, dyspnoea and fatigue. The physical examination was unremarkable, and there was no known relevant family history. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated significant concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with markedly reduced native myocardial T1 values. No significant coronary artery abnormalities were identified, raising suspicion of an infiltrative or metabolic cardiomyopathy. Plasma α-galactosidase A activity was markedly reduced at 0.3 nmol/mL/h (reference interval, 2.0–10.0 nmol/mL/h), which, together with the compatible cardiac imaging findings, strongly supported a diagnosis of Fabry disease, although molecular confirmation was unavailable. This case highlights a cardiac-predominant presentation strongly supportive of Fabry disease in a young Malaysian adult without documented classical extracardiac manifestations or a known relevant family history. It underscores the importance of considering Fabry disease in young patients with otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy and characteristic cardiac magnetic resonance findings. Early recognition is important to facilitate molecular confirmation, family screening and timely consideration of disease-specific management before irreversible organ damage develops.

title: Development of a Modified FDM-Based Bioprinter with Optimized Extrusion Parameters for High-Fidelity Alginate Bioinks and Aortic Valve Scaffold Manufacturing
authors: Omer Yaskeceli; Kadir Aydın
journal: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON APPLIED AND THEORETICAL MECHANICS
abstract: Aortic valve disease is a major cause of cardiovascular deaths worldwide. Aortic stenosis increases the workload on the heart and severely alters hemodynamic function by impairing effective blood flow. In recent years, extrusion-based bioprinting technologies have made significant progress in producing patient-specific, biocompatible cardiovascular structures, opening up new opportunities for advanced therapeutic applications. In this study, a commercially available FDM-type 3D printer (ENDER-3 Pro) was mechanically and electronically modified into a fully functional, low-cost bioprinter capable of depositing alginate-gelatin hydrogels with high structural fidelity, despite their low viscosity. The redesigned system integrates a NEMA-17 driven syringe extrusion module equipped with a TR8X8 lead screw, enabling high-resolution pressure-controlled deposition of viscoelastic bioinks. A three-leaflet aortic valve geometry was digitally reconstructed and simplified using Fusion 360 to ensure printability while preserving essential anatomical features. The printing parameters were systematically investigated according to the alginate-based bioinks and set to a nozzle diameter (0.6 mm), layer height (0.6 mm), extrusion multiplier (0.02), and printing speed (5 mm/s). Quantitative shape fidelity assessment, including top-down geometric deviation analysis, confirmed that the bioprinted aortic valve constructs successfully maintained the nominal CAD boundaries. By dynamically optimizing slicing parameters, specifically the extrusion multiplier, rheologically driven deformations such as excessive lateral spreading were effectively mitigated. Although comprehensive evaluation of hemodynamic performance requires future in vitro experiments and coupled fluid–structure interaction (FSI) simulations, the present study establishes a robust and accessible biofabrication framework capable of producing highly complex cardiovascular geometries. Cost-effective and adaptable bioprinting platforms, derived from consumer-grade fused deposition modeling (FDM) systems, can achieve the geometric fidelity and structural stability necessary for advanced cardiovascular tissue engineering. This approach significantly enhances the accessibility of high-precision bioprinting technologies, thereby facilitating broader adoption in both research and translational applications.

title: Nitric Oxide and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Chronic Heart Failure: A Narrative Review
authors: Igor Belenichev; Olena Aliyeva; Nina Bukhtiyarova; Victor Ryzhenko; Kyuho Yi
abstract: Chronic heart failure (CHF) remains a leading cause of hospital admission, disability, and cardiovascular death despite major advances in guideline-directed therapy.Beyond hemodynamic impairment and neurohormonal activation, CHF is increasingly understood as a disorder of endothelial dysfunction, nitrosoredox imbalance, mitochondrial injury, energetic failure, and regulated cell death.Nitric oxide (NO) signaling and mitochondrial homeostasis are interconnected components of this broader pathophysiologic network.Under physiologic conditions, endothelial NO synthase-derived NO contributes to vascular tone, coronary microvascular regulation, and myocardial signaling.In CHF, reduced endothelial NO bioavailability may coexist with increased formation of reactive nitrogen species, particularly in inflammatory and oxidizing conditions.The resulting nitroso-redox imbalance can interact with mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction, altered calcium handling, oxidative stress, and regulated cell death, although the relative contribution of these mechanisms varies across heart failure phenotypes and disease states.Guidelinedirected therapies, including angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, evidence-based beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, improve clinical outcomes through established neurohormonal, renal, and hemodynamic mechanisms.Experimental and translational evidence suggests that some of these therapies may also influence endothelial, redox, metabolic, or mitochondrial pathways, although the clinical contribution of these secondary effects remains incompletely defined.These mechanistic observations have also motivated investigation of therapies that more directly target endothelial, redox, or mitochondrial abnormalities.Hypertril (1-(beta-phenylethyl)-4-amino-1,2,4-triazolium bromide) is an investigational compound with reported beta-blocking, NO-related, and metabolic effects in experimental models; however, the available evidence remains predominantly preclinical and does not establish clinical efficacy in human CHF.This narrative review examines NO dysregulation and mitochondrial dysfunction as interconnected components of CHF pathophysiology, considers their relationship to contemporary pharmacotherapy, and discusses the translational limitations and research priorities associated with targeting these pathways.

title: Antecedents and consequences of Green-tech FDI in emerging markets
authors: Zhuoran Liu
abstract: As environmental pressures intensify, attracting sustainable foreign direct investment (FDI), particularly green-tech FDI, has become a critical pathway for emerging markets to achieve environmental sustainability. However, existing research remains fragmented, offering limited insights into why green-tech FDI enters emerging markets and how it affects regional green innovation. This thesis addresses these gaps by systematically examining both the antecedents and consequences of green-tech FDI through three empirical studies using regional data from China. Study 1 and Study 2 focus on the antecedents of green-tech FDI. Study 1 examines how host-country conditions can attract green-tech FDI, highlighting the role of environmental management information disclosure (EMID) by domestic firms in reducing information gaps and strengthening green market–seeking motives. Study 2 shifts attention to the active decision-making of green-tech FDI, showing that under uncertainty, green-tech foreign investors engage in identity-based bandwagon learning by imitating peers with similar green identities, thereby mitigating investment risks. Study 3 turns to the consequences of green-tech FDI. It demonstrates that, due to the technological complexity of green innovation and limited absorptive capacity in emerging markets, green-tech FDI may generate crowding-out effects rather than purely positive spillovers. Adopting a network perspective, the study further finds that universities play a key moderating role: through broad linkages and deep collaborations, they help mitigate negative spillovers and facilitate the diffusion of green technologies. Together, the three studies advance the literature on sustainable FDI by differentiating green-tech FDI from general FDI and identifying the specific mechanisms that shape its entry decisions and local innovation outcomes. Practically, the findings provide guidance for emerging-market governments and firms on how to attract and manage sustainable investment, balance growth with environmental objectives, and strengthen local innovation ecosystems.

title: Combating Data and Target Shifts in Visual Tasks
authors: Zhaorui Tan
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep learning models for visual tasks has led to significant progress in many domains. However, a key challenge remains: ensuring that models can generalize effectively to unseen samples or novel classes, especially in real-world scenarios where training data-target pairs are often limited or unavailable, and test data may exhibit shifts in both data and targets. This thesis addresses the problem of shifts across data and targets, proposing novel methods to improve model generalization and transferability in complex settings. The thesis identifies the different shift scenarios for visual tasks and presents their problem forms. The research first relaxes the static target distribution assumption in Multi-Domain Generalization (mDG) tasks, introducing the General Multi-Domain Generalization (GMDG) objective to improve generalization under varying data shifts. Specifically, Extensive experiments validate that GMDG is feasible for classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Further considering extreme target distribution shifts where even unknown novel classes emerge, the study also explores logical regularization techniques for tasks such as Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), mDG+GCD, and Class Incremental Learning (CIL), proposing a sample-based logical regularization term (L-Reg) to enhance data-, target-, and all-shift generalization. Additionally, a partial logic framework is introduced to address challenges in CIL, enabling models to retain room for unknown classes during training. This is further extended by the Partial-Logic Regularization (PL-Reg), which improves generalization across GCD, mDG+GCD, and transferability for CIL tasks. Furthermore, the thesis proposes a novel Semantic-aware Data Augmentation (SADA) framework for cross-modality generalization in text-to-image synthesis (T2Isyn), text-image retrieval (TIR), and image-text retrieval (ITR) tasks. This framework ensures semantic preservation across text and image modalities, improving both semantic consistency and image quality in cross-modality tasks. The methods proposed in this thesis offer significant advancements in visual generalization and transfer scenarios, providing theoretical insights and practical solutions for handling data shifts, target shifts, and multi-modalities in complex scenarios. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating their superior performance across a range of tasks.

title: Depth of Processing, learner aptitude, and the acquisition of L2 English grammatical structures
authors: Shweta Nigam
abstract: Depth of Processing (DoP) is central to several models of instructed second language acquisition (ISLA) (Leow, 2015). While DoP has been extensively examined in vocabulary learning (e.g., Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001), its role in the acquisition of grammatical structures, particularly through oral and audio-visual modalities remains comparatively underexplored. Drawing on the Levels of Processing framework (Craik & Lockhart, 1972), this study investigated whether task-induced processing depth influences the acquisition of third conditionals and comparatives, and whether language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) predicts learning gains. Using a pretest–posttest design, four intact classes involving 108 Grade 8 EFL learners in India were assigned to one of the three experimental conditions differing in level and type of processing: Low DoP, High DoP Explicit, and High DoP Implicit. The treatment task required the participants to listen to an audio-visual story containing the target structures (third conditionals and comparatives) and complete analytic tasks (varying in different groups) before listening to the story for a second time. The oral performance of the participants was analysed for accuracy, and frequency of use of the target structures. A grammaticality judgement test (GJT) and an elicited imitation task (EIT) were used to assess the participants’ gains in the knowledge of the target structures. In addition, language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) was measured and modelled as a predictor of gain scores. Results showed a significant effect of processing condition on GJT performance with the High DoP Implicit group outperforming the High DoP Explicit group on total scores and comparatives. In contrast, ANCOVA analyses indicated no significant group differences on EIT outcomes once pretest performance was controlled, with pretest scores strongly predicting posttest performance. In oral production, processing effects were structure-specific: the Low DoP group showed greater accuracy gains for comparatives, while both High DoP groups revealed increased frequency of use of third conditionals. However, across all four measures, multiple regression analyses indicated that LLAMA B, D, and F did not significantly predict gain scores. Overall, the findings support a processing-by-structure pattern: deeper processing benefits were most evident for the more salient structure (comparatives) on an explicit, written measure, whereas complex, low-salience forms (third conditionals) showed limited accuracy change but increased frequency of use under deeper processing.

title: A UAV-Based Framework for Community-Scale Residential Building Energy Modelling in China
authors: Mengfan Jin
abstract: With increasing emphasis on energy efficiency and carbon emission reduction in the building sector, rapid and scalable energy modelling of existing buildings is critical for retrofit projects and policy development. Conventional surveys, data collection and energy modelling processes remain labour-intensive and impractical for large-scale applications, and energy modelling often dominates project time and cost. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with high-resolution and infrared cameras now offer fast and safe exterior surveys, showing great potential in building energy assessments. Yet, a systematic framework for UAV integration, from image capture through processing to inputs for building energy simulation, has not been established. This research addresses these challenges by developing a structured framework for community-scale building energy modelling, which integrates UAV photogrammetry to accelerate data acquisition, reduce labour, and shorten energy modelling time for retrofit projects. The framework is designed to minimise prior data requirements while maximising automation and retaining sufficient accuracy and reliability. It also addressed systemic issues, such as the lack of data necessary to fully exploit the potential of available technologies in the context of this study. To achieve this research objective, a mixed-methodology approach, combining desk studies and fieldwork, was adopted. First, a comprehensive review of UAV-based building energy studies mapped the current applications and available tools, proposing a preliminary framework. Fieldwork then encompassed a pilot study and a detailed case study. In the pilot test, a single building was surveyed to identify an optimal toolchain for flight planning, image capture, photogrammetric reconstruction, model generation, and selection of a simulation platform. The resulting refined framework was applied to a case study of a 39-building community, and it was demonstrated that further automation was necessary. The potential for automation was then further explored. Geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning techniques were compared, and the combination that best balanced accuracy and processing time was selected for 3D model generation and window-to-wall ratio (WWR) extraction. In parallel, an archetype library of residential buildings in the Hot Summer Cold Winter (HSCW) zone in China was compiled to facilitate the assignment of thermal parameters. Finally, a reusable community-scale building energy modelling (CBEM) workflow was assembled in Grasshopper using Ladybug Tools components to process the aforementioned inputs. In conclusion, this study integrates UAV photogrammetry, GIS-based geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and graphical programming to develop an UAV-CBEM framework. The outcomes establish a foundation for scalable UAV-based building energy assessments, enhancing applicability in data-limited and large-scale settings worldwide.

title: Spectral Materialism: Encounters with land-time-scapes
authors: Nightingale, Sam
abstract: This transdisciplinary, practice-based PhD introduces spectral materialism through art-based research encounters with ecologically and historically stratified land-time-scapes shaped by hypersalinity and colonial terraforming. Centred in the semi-arid Mallee (southeastern Australia) and read through echoes with California’s Imperial Valley, the project examines how spectral time—the co-presence and haunting of other temporalities—manifests in the material conditions of salt, soil, water, plants, and infrastructures. It asks how learning from geological, First Nations, colonial, and ecological pasts can orient responsibilities in unsettled futures. Treating the present as a crisis of time as much as a crisis of matter, the thesis critiques linear-progressive temporalities bound to Western modernity and extractive regimes. In response, spectral materialism is developed as both a conceptual framework and a critical creative methodology. Through alchemical media experiments with salt crystals, hypersaline soils, and halophytes, photography is reconfigured as a site-responsive, process-oriented practice. Salt is engaged as a material agent and ‘time-crystal’ whose phase shifts—dissolution, saturation, precipitation, crystallisation, evaporation—form a meta-chemistry that refracts deep-marine pasts, settler-colonial irrigation infrastructures, and contemporary dust into processual renderings of time. Methodologically, the project advances attunement as a mode of sensing and responsiveness to forces that are not always immediately perceptible yet are materially active. Field notes appear as para-writing, interrupting linear narration so that heterogeneous times co-present themselves within the text. The thesis is guided by First Nations temporalities—time as relational and in place—while remaining accountable to ethical limits and protocols. The contribution is twofold: a theoretical articulation of spectral materialism as a way to think time otherwise, and a set of site-responsive methods for engaging elemental media in saline environments. Together, they generate materially grounded accounts of spectral presences and open alternative pathways for knowing, sensing, and relating within land-time-scapes marked by enduring colonial and ecological afterlives amid planetary change.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND COMMERCIALIZATION OF COMPUTATIONAL METHODS TO ACCELERATE DERMATOLOGICAL DISCOVERY
authors: Jasson Makkar
abstract: The skin is the largest and outermost organ that surrounds the human body and provides a physical barrier that protects the more delicate internal tissues from the harsh surrounding environment. Over the course of evolution, specialized structures have also arisen in the skin, including sweat and sebaceous glands, nails and claws, and hair follicles. The hair follicle is a multi-lineage mini-organ that is a critical component in defining mammalian species. The gain of function derived from hair and fur benefited these species for millennia due to its insulative and protective properties, mechanosensing function, and ability to serve as camouflage. Current approaches to assess these fibers are generally non-quantitative or are low throughput due to technical limitations of ‘splitting hairs’. We developed a novel deep learning-based computer vision approach for the high throughput quantification of individual hair fibers at a high resolution. Our innovative computer vision tool can distinguish and extract overlapping fibers for quantification of multivariate features including length, width, and color to generate single-hair phenomes (shPhenome) of diverse conditions across the lifespan of mice. Using our tool, we explored the effects of hormone signaling, genetic modifications, and aging on hair follicle output. These analyses revealed novel hair phenotypes as a result of endocrinological, developmental, and aging-related alterations in the fur coats of mice. This tool was then adapted to capture more nuanced hair phenotypes, such as curvature, in a variety of mouse models harboring genetic perturbations. Commercialization of the deep hair phenomics technology presented a unique opportunity to pursue research translation, transforming fundamental biological research into marketable products. Much like the traditional academic route, the path to commercialization requires consistent and continuous iteration, testing of hypotheses, and allowing data to influence and lead subsequent actions. However, as opposed to the pursuit of knowledge, translating research into market-ready solutions requires a focus on consumer needs and the identification of market opportunities. Additionally, the shift in incentive structure requires commercial ventures to prioritize intellectual property protection, alter capital and resource allocation, and seek alternative fundraising sources. The entrepreneurial foundation built through this process culminated in the filing of a provisional patent and establishment of a startup company, kerat Inc. This journey illuminated the multifaceted challenges inherent in closing the gap between academic innovation and commercially viable goods, requiring simultaneous advancement of technical capabilities, adaptation to market dynamics, and fabrication of business infrastructure. Overall, the culmination of work presented in this dissertation sheds light on the importance of quantitatively assessing hair fiber properties to capture the biological phenomena that underlie this fundamental feature of mammalian skin. These findings also highlight the capabilities of this methodology for identifying perturbations in normal growth, potentially indicative of disease or dysfunction. Lastly, this showcased the potential of this technology’s commercial use cases in both the cosmetics and diagnostics industries.

title: Contested urbanisms: The politics of heritage and housing in Jakarta’s kampungs
authors: Binte Masron, Irna Nurlina
abstract: Do heritage-making projects resist or advance gentrification in Southeast Asia? Like other Global South cities, contested urbanisms chequer Jakarta’s postcolonial urban landscape. Competing ideas about urban development manifest in various ways of seeing and producing the city, as demonstrated by evictions, revitalisation projects, and informal housing. Increased evictions of urban villages (urban kampungs) between 2013 and 2018 in Jakarta saw growing grassroots heritage movements as part of a spectrum of resistance to top-down urban management by state and private sector actors who also stake their claims on what ‘heritage’ is. These tensions amongst the political projects of various actors led me to ask: how do heritage-making projects of/by urban villages affect housing conditions in Jakarta, with reference to gentrification-led displacement? Using ethnographic methods and thematic analysis, I delve into the constructions of heritage, the impact of heritage-making on housing security for residents, and the broader political impact of heritage-making from above and below in Jakarta’s Kota Tua and two of its kampungs, Luar Batang and Pekojan. I argue that the dominant heritage constructions in Kota Tua demonstrate a top-down logic that emphasises infrastructure and the built environment with strong private sector presence, which impact the kampungs in varied ways. Findings showed that top-down heritage-making demonstrates higher likelihood of driving gentrification through the commodification of space, prioritising capital and material values. Residents and their advocates employ heritage-making from below in various forms to reclaim their place in the city as they face various forms of displacement, with unanticipated consequences. The processes of heritage-making from above and below reveal the connections and disjunctures between different authorities which subaltern actors work through, producing new politics that contest or entrench existing conditions. The findings contribute to the theorising of the politics of gentrification in heritage and urban studies, and a deeper understanding of Jakarta’s Old Town.

title: From Sparse to Dense: Label-Efficient Weakly Supervised Segmentation for Images and Videos
authors: Wang, Jian
abstract: Obtaining high-quality annotated data has become a primary bottleneck for training deep learning models, particularly for dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation and video salient object segmentation. The demand for meticulous, pixel-level labeling makes fully-supervised approaches prohibitively expensive and limits their scalability. This thesis directly confronts this issue by proposing and systematically investigating a label-efficient "sparse-to-dense'' paradigm. The core objective is to develop innovative frameworks that can learn from sparse, inexpensive weak supervision—such as image-level tags or scribbles—and intelligently propagate this minimal information to generate complete, pixel-accurate dense predictions. The major part of this thesis focuses on the "sparse-to-dense'' challenge within Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS) for images, where models learn from only image-level tags. Dominant approaches rely on Class Activation Maps (CAMs) as initial object seeds. However, CAMs inherently activate only the most discriminative object regions, leading to incomplete pseudo-labels. This gives rise to the central problem of activation densification: the critical process of expanding these sparse activations to cover the full extent of an object. Our research addresses this challenge through a progressive, multi-faceted strategy. Our exploration begins with a foundational framework (C3) designed to rectify the intrinsic flaws of initial CAMs. We propose a synergistic mutual calibration method. This method leverages the discrepancies between the two maps to generate local prototypes, which are simultaneously utilized to complete missing object parts and suppress background noise, yielding a significantly more accurate and complete initial seed. This foundational work immediately reveals the limitation of single-prototype instability and its inability to capture diverse features. Building on this foundation, we then develop architecture-specific strategies to address deeper limitations of the prototype-based approach. For Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (C4), the use of a single prototype proves insufficient to capture significant intra-class variation. In response, we introduce an Optimal Transport (OT)-assisted framework that effectively mines multiple, diverse prototypes, thereby yielding more comprehensive activation maps. However, while C4 solves the intra-class diversity problem, the inherent local context constraint of the CNN architecture becomes the new bottleneck, fundamentally limiting the quality of globally-aware feature extraction needed for optimal multi-prototype assignment. This limitation necessitates a shift in architectural focus from CNNs to Vision Transformers. In the ViT architecture (C5), a new challenge arises where the token gap between the discriminative class token and varied patch tokens leads to incomplete activation. To bridge this gap, we leverage a tailored application of Optimal Transport, where the algorithm is tasked with learning a comprehensive proxy to ensure complete object activation. Despite these architectural advances (C3-C5), the overall WSSS performance hit a ceiling. This is fundamentally limited by the sparse supervision of class labels, which cannot provide precise boundary information. To break this ceiling, our WSSS exploration culminates in a universal enhancement strategy (C6) that transcends architecture-specific designs by leveraging Visual Foundation Models (VFMs). We resolve the conflict between the discriminative nature of initial CAMs and the VFM's need for holistic prompts. By modeling the CAM foreground as a graph and employing spectral analysis, our method intelligently selects a diverse set of prompt points that represent the overall structure of the foreground object. This guides the VFM to generate superior, boundary-aware supervision that can universally enhance any WSSS pipeline. Subsequently, the thesis extends the "sparse-to-dense'' paradigm to the dynamic domain of video, addressing Weakly Supervised Video Salient Object Segmentation (WSVSOS) (C7) from sparse scribble annotations. In this specific context, the challenge evolves into spatio-temporal densification, which requires both full-object coverage within each frame and temporal consistency across the video sequences. To this end, we introduce the core CFMR framework, which utilizes Spatio-Temporal co-regulation. This framework is subsequently enhanced (CFMR+) by integrating the VFM guidance strategy from C6, which provides high-quality spatial priors essential for ensuring both high spatial detail and inter-frame consistency. By enforcing both intra-frame and cross-frame consistency between these two streams, our method effectively propagates the sparse initial signal to generate dense and temporally coherent saliency masks. In conclusion, this thesis presents a comprehensive and cohesive investigation into label-efficient segmentation tasks, offering a suite of innovative and effective strategies for the "sparse-to-dense'' challenge. Our work establishes a progressive roadmap that systematically overcomes architectural and semantic limitations, culminating in highly robust and generalized densification pipelines. Our extensive experimental results on standard benchmarks validate the state-of-the-art performance of these methods, providing robust solutions to a long-standing problem in the computer vision field.

title: Unsupervised Deep-learning Methods for Low-dose Computed Tomography Reconstruction
authors: An, Ran
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) has become an indispensable imaging technique in medical diagnostics and industrial applications, owing to its non-invasive nature and high resolution in visualizing object internal structures. While X-ray CT (X-ray computed tomography) significantly enhances lesion detection capabilities, excessive exposure to X-ray radiation raises substantial health concerns, including elevated cancer risks and potential genetic damage. Although low-dose CT (LDCT) protocols reduce radiation safety concerns, they inevitably introduce severe noise and artifacts, which might compromise diagnostic accuracy. Recent advances in supervised deep learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in LDCT reconstruction. However, the reliance on paired training data severely limits their deployment in practical CT applications. This fundamental constraint highlights the critical importance of developing unsupervised reconstruction methods. Although existing unsupervised LDCT methods have made notable progress, they still face challenges requiring systematic solutions. This thesis makes three contributions to advance the field of unsupervised LDCT reconstruction: 1. Current dual-domain self-supervised LDCT denoising methods typically neglect the heterogeneity of the non-stationary Gaussian noise levels in low-dose sinograms and usually treat them as common images without appropriately controlling the denoising strength. The denoisers employed by them, which are based on classic convolutional neural networks (CNN), will lead to blurring artifacts in the reconstructed images if directly used for sinogram denoising. In addition, the denoising strength in the sinogram and image domains must be well-balanced to avoid introducing over-blurring or secondary artifacts in the reconstructed images, but existing approaches do not focus on this crucial point. To address these limitations, this thesis proposes a novel end-to-end dual-domain self-supervised framework for LDCT denoising. It employs Dropblock layers to adaptively localize the effect of convolution for sinogram denoising and sets a weighted average between the denoised sinograms and their noisy counterparts to better control the denoising strength, thus effectively reducing the blurring artifacts and leading to a well-balanced dual-domain denoising. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of the proposed method. 2. Existing normalizing flows (NFs)-based unsupervised LDCT reconstruction methods face challenges in both image quality and computational efficiency. On one hand, they typically utilize a two-way transformation strategy between noisy images and latent variables, which could easily lead to detail loss and secondary artifacts in the reconstructed images. On the other hand, training NFs on high-resolution CT images is computationally intensive. Although conditional normalizing flows (CNFs) can mitigate computational costs by learning conditional probabilities, existing approaches rely on labeled data for conditionalization, leaving unsupervised CNFs-based LDCT reconstruction a challenge. To tackle these issues, this thesis proposes a novel unsupervised LDCT iterative reconstruction algorithm based on CNFs. The proposed method employs a strict one-way transformation strategy during the alternating optimization in the dual spaces to prevent detail loss and secondary artifacts, and proposes a novel unsupervised conditionalization strategy for CNFs, thus achieving efficient training and inference on high-resolution images. The proposed method illustrates high-quality and relatively fast unsupervised reconstruction. Experiments across two datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method by rivaling several state-of-the-art methods. 3. Current diffusion model-based LDCT reconstruction methods solely employ the prior distributions learned from normal-dose CT data but neglect the valuable priors in low-dose data, which contain information about the characteristics of low-dose noise and artifacts. In addition, their reconstruction speed suffers from multiple sampling steps, presenting low efficiency. Breaking new ground in prior utilization, this thesis proposes a novel unsupervised LDCT iterative reconstruction algorithm based on dual denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM), which leverages both normal-dose and low-dose priors. Specifically, the proposed method employs two DDPMs to learn the prior distributions from normal-dose and low-dose images, respectively, and incorporates them into a joint iterative reconstruction framework. To accelerate the reconstruction, partial diffusion sampling and single-pass deterministic reconstruction strategy are utilized in the proposed method, as well as the spaced OS-SART approaches. Experiments at different dose levels demonstrate the outstanding performance and fast speed of the proposed reconstruction algorithm. Through these innovations and contributions, this thesis addresses some significant challenges in current deep-learning-based unsupervised LDCT reconstruction methods, and proposes three novel unsupervised reconstruction algorithms. The proposed methods effectively improve the performance and efficiency of LDCT reconstruction under different unsupervised learning conditions, and provide some new perspectives and inspirations for future research.

authors: Ji Yun; Ville Tiusanen; Konsta Karttunen; Divyesh Patel; Esa Pitkänen; Biswajyoti Sahu
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Overview This record accompanies the manuscript "Deep learning reveals distinct and complementary cis-regulatory grammar from STARR-seq and lentiMPRA". The archive contains processed data, analysis workflows, selected model artifacts, source records, and figure-level outputs used to compare episomal genomic STARR-seq and integrated lentivirus-based MPRA in HepG2 cells. The study integrates assay signal comparison, cCRE and epigenomic annotation, transcription factor ChIP-seq correlation, motif enrichment, regression-based motif activity analysis, and sequence-based deep learning to characterize shared and assay-specific cis-regulatory grammar. Contents This release includes: processed STARR-seq and lentiMPRA analysis inputs; DeepSTARR FASTA/TSV model input files; lentiMPRA probe-level and STARR-seq peak-level activity tables; selected raw/source files redistributed with the release; public accession tables and source-resource inventories; JASPAR 2024 motif files and transcription factor annotation tables; workflow scripts for data preparation, signal comparison, motif analysis, model training and evaluation, and supplementary analyses; MEIRLOP and GimmeMotifs result tables and figure outputs; trained DeepSTARR baseline model files, held-out test splits, predictions, and performance summaries; manuscript figures and supplementary outputs; environment/version notes; MANIFEST.tsv and checksums.tsv for file inventory and SHA256 verification. Workflow Modules The release is organized into the following workflow modules: 01_data_preparation 02_signal_comparison 03_chip_epigenome_correlation 04_meirlop 05_gimmemotifs 06_deepstarr 07_supplementary_features MPRALegnet.tar.gz Each module contains the scripts, intermediate outputs, and documentation required to reproduce the corresponding analyses. Scope and External Inputs This archive provides a reproducible snapshot of the computational analyses performed for the manuscript. Original public datasets are not redistributed and should be downloaded from their respective repositories using the accession tables and references provided in the manuscript and accompanying source files. Large third-party resources, including the GRCh38 reference genome and selected ENCODE ChIP-seq and epigenomic bigWig files, are documented but not bundled. Their expected locations and regeneration instructions are described in the workflow README files. This release includes DeepSTARR model artifacts. MPRALegNet training, attribution analyses, TF-MoDISco results, and associated model files are documented as deferred components and are not included in this release.
